e-602.knowledge_point: Finding an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Parametric Curve
e-602.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14039829/assets/834eff403ac2a6f696e104ec914cac1b951f8a6d989e11c0e9f2576ac9e7f0d8.png)

Find an integral expression for the arc length of the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=1-t, \quad y= \dfrac{2}{3} t^{3/2}, \qquad t\in[0,1].
$$
e-602.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \sqrt{ \left( \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2 + \left( \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2}\:\textrm{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-t)=-1\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3/2})={t}^{1/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{{(-1)}^{2}+{({t}^{1/2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1+t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

e-7130.knowledge_point: Finding an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Parametric Curve Containing Special Functions
e-7130.problem:
Find the expression that gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=t, \, y=\ln{(\cos{t})}$
from $t=0$ to $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ (see graph below).

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14039829/assets/48de26c11ae08afb45ec19ee56e770f7418f9be2afb8ee7dd46a0d1136cb125b.png)
e-7130.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \sqrt{ \left( \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2 + \left( \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2}\:\textrm{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡t))=-\operatorname{tan}⁡t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{(1)}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{tan}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{1+{tan}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{sec}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sec}⁡t\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

e-603.knowledge_point: Finding the Arc Length of a Parametric Curve
e-603.problem:
Find the arc length of the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=e^t(\cos{t}+\sin{t}), \quad y=e^t(\cos{t}-\sin{t}) , \quad t\in \left[0,\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right].
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14039829/assets/15d185178bf8882f837c19361d630c0e537e145ca2337cad4655677255d0348a.png)
e-603.worked_solution:
Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)) \\  & ={e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+{e}^{t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\  & =2{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)) \\  & ={e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+{e}^{t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\  & =-2{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{(2{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(-2{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{4{e}^{2t}({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}2{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{e}^{t}{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =2({e}^{\pi /4}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

a

b
∫01t18t2+8dt

2∫01t3t2+2dt

∫01t18t2+24t+8dt

decision.explanation: Arc length is L=∫₀¹√((x′(t))²+(y′(t))²) dt. Here x′=3t²+2t and y′=3t²−2t, so their squared sum is 18t⁴+8t². Since t≥0, the speed is t√(18t²+8), giving option b.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x={t}^{3}+{t}^{2},\,y={t}^{3}-{t}^{2}$
from $t=0$ to $t=1$ ?
after.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}+{t}^{2})=3{t}^{2}+2t\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-{t}^{2})=3{t}^{2}-2t\,.\end{aligned}

Question 1
?

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=t3+t2,y=t3−t2 from t=0 to t=1 ?

a
∫01t9t2+4dt
b
∫01t18t2+8dt
c
2∫01t3t2+2dt
d
2∫01t9t2+2t+4dt
e
∫01t18t2+24t+8dt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To compute the arc length L of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

Computing the derivatives of x and y, we have

dxdt=ddt(t3+t2)=3t2+2t and dydt=ddt(t3−t2)=3t2−2t.

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=∫01(3t2+2t)2+(3t2−2t)2dt=∫019t4+12t3+4t2+9t4−12t3+4t2dt=∫0118t4+8t2dt=∫01t18t2+8dt.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms option b. The derivatives are 3t²+2t and 3t²−2t; squaring and adding cancels the cross terms, giving 18t⁴+8t². Since t≥0 on [0,1], the arc-length integrand is t√(18t²+8).

content.knowledge_point: Finding an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Parametric Curve
content.problem:
Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x={t}^{3}+{t}^{2},\,y={t}^{3}-{t}^{2}$
from $t=0$ to $t=1$ ?
content.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}+{t}^{2})=3{t}^{2}+2t\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-{t}^{2})=3{t}^{2}-2t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{{(3{t}^{2}+2t)}^{2}+{(3{t}^{2}-2t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{9{t}^{4}+12{t}^{3}+4{t}^{2}+9{t}^{4}-12{t}^{3}+4{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{18{t}^{4}+8{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}t\sqrt{18{t}^{2}+8}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 2
?

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=3t3+5,y=t2−5t from t=−1 to t=2 ?

a
∫−1281t4+4t2−20t+25dt
b
∫−129t4+4t2−20t+5dt
c
2∫−129t4+t2−5t+6dt
d
3∫−1227t4+4t2−t+6dt
e
∫−1285t4−20t+25dt
Submit

decision.explanation: Using the parametric arc-length formula, x′=9t² and y′=2t−5. Thus (x′)²+(y′)²=81t⁴+4t²−20t+25. Integrating its square root from −1 to 2 gives option a.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=3{t}^{3}+5,\,y={t}^{2}-5t$
from $t=-1$ to $t=2$ ?
after.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{3}+5)=9{t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-5t)=2t-5.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}\sqrt{(9{t}^{2})^{2}+(2t-5)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}\sqrt{81{t}^{4}+4{t}^{2}-20t+25}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=3t3+5,y=t2−5t from t=−1 to t=2 ?

a
∫−1281t4+4t2−20t+25dt
b
∫−129t4+4t2−20t+5dt
c
2∫−129t4+t2−5t+6dt
d
3∫−1227t4+4t2−t+6dt
e
∫−1285t4−20t+25dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the arc length L of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

Computing the derivatives of x and y, we have

dxdt=ddt(3t3+5)=9t2 and dydt=ddt(t2−5t)=2t−5.

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=∫−12(9t2)2+(2t−5)2dt=∫−1281t4+4t2−20t+25dt.

content.knowledge_point: Finding an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Parametric Curve
content.problem:
Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=3{t}^{3}+5,\,y={t}^{2}-5t$
from $t=-1$ to $t=2$ ?
content.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{3}+5)=9{t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-5t)=2t-5.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}\sqrt{(9{t}^{2})^{2}+(2t-5)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}\sqrt{81{t}^{4}+4{t}^{2}-20t+25}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=t3−4,y=2t from t=−2 to t=0 (shown above)?

a
∫−209t4+3dt
b
3∫−203t4+1dt
c
∫−20t4+tdt
d
∫−20t4+2dt
e
∫−209t4+4dt
Submit

decision.explanation: The arc length is the integral of √((x′)²+(y′)²). Since x′=3t² and y′=2, the speed is √(9t⁴+4). Integrating from −2 to 0 gives option e.

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14039829/assets/ae210abc4028440aa9c822510d68f0ab0b8ba4b9f5806dd299149e953ccd1b21.png)

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x={t}^{3}-4,\,y=2t$
from $t=-2$ to $t=0$ (shown above)?
after.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-4)=3{t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)=2.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}\sqrt{(3{t}^{2})^{2}+(2)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}\sqrt{9{t}^{4}+4}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=t3−4,y=2t from t=−2 to t=0 (shown above)?

a
∫−209t4+3dt
b
3∫−203t4+1dt
c
∫−20t4+tdt
d
∫−20t4+2dt
e
∫−209t4+4dt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To compute the arc length L of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

Computing the derivatives of x and y, we have

dxdt=ddt(t3−4)=3t2 and dydt=ddt(2t)=2.

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=∫−20(3t2)2+(2)2dt=∫−209t4+4dt.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms that x′=3t² and y′=2, so the arc length is ∫₋₂⁰√(9t⁴+4) dt, matching option e. The displayed incorrect submission selected c.

content.knowledge_point: Finding an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Parametric Curve
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14039829/assets/ae210abc4028440aa9c822510d68f0ab0b8ba4b9f5806dd299149e953ccd1b21.png)

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x={t}^{3}-4,\,y=2t$
from $t=-2$ to $t=0$ (shown above)?
content.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-4)=3{t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)=2.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}\sqrt{(3{t}^{2})^{2}+(2)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}\sqrt{9{t}^{4}+4}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=3t2,y=5t from t=0 to t=1 (shown above)?

a
∫016t2+1dt
b
5∫01t2+5dt
c
4∫0136t2+5tdt
d
2∫0118t2−12dt
e
∫0136t2+25dt
Submit

decision.explanation: For parametric arc length, integrate √((x′)²+(y′)²). Here x′=6t and y′=5, so the speed is √(36t²+25). With bounds 0 and 1, this matches option e.

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14039829/assets/0a58808ee9b20e201d1ea8a31683f742e02f739127640de2fea87ce4757e7901.png)

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=3{t}^{2},\,y=5t$
from $t=0$ to $t=1$ (shown above)?
after.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2})=6t\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5t)=5.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{(6t)^{2}+(5)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{36{t}^{2}+25}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

after.html:
Question 4
?

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=3t2,y=5t from t=0 to t=1 (shown above)?

a
∫016t2+1dt
b
5∫01t2+5dt
c
4∫0136t2+5tdt
d
2∫0118t2−12dt
e
∫0136t2+25dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the arc length L of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

Computing the derivatives of x and y, we have

dxdt=ddt(3t2)=6t and dydt=ddt(5t)=5.

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=∫01(6t)2+(5)2dt=∫0136t2+25dt.

content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14039829/assets/0a58808ee9b20e201d1ea8a31683f742e02f739127640de2fea87ce4757e7901.png)

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=3{t}^{2},\,y=5t$
from $t=0$ to $t=1$ (shown above)?
content.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2})=6t\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5t)=5.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{(6t)^{2}+(5)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{36{t}^{2}+25}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 5
?

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=t−1,y=t2+2 from t=−1 to t=2 ?

a
∫−124+t+4t2dt
b
∫−121+4t+4t2dt
c
∫−12t+4t2dt
d
∫−124+4t+t2dt
e
∫−121+4t2dt
Submit

decision.explanation: The derivatives are x′=1 and y′=2t. The arc length is therefore ∫₋₁²√((1)²+(2t)²) dt = ∫₋₁²√(1+4t²) dt, matching option e.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=t-1,\,y={t}^{2}+2$
from $t=-1$ to $t=2$ ?
after.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-1)=1\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+2)=2t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}\sqrt{{(1)}^{2}+{(2t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}\sqrt{1+4{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=t−1,y=t2+2 from t=−1 to t=2 ?

a
∫−124+t+4t2dt
b
∫−121+4t+4t2dt
c
∫−12t+4t2dt
d
∫−124+4t+t2dt
e
∫−121+4t2dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the arc length L of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

Computing the derivatives of x and y, we have

dxdt=ddt(t−1)=1 and dydt=ddt(t2+2)=2t.

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=∫−12(1)2+(2t)2dt=∫−121+4t2dt.

content.knowledge_point: Finding an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Parametric Curve
content.problem:
Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=t-1,\,y={t}^{2}+2$
from $t=-1$ to $t=2$ ?
content.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-1)=1\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+2)=2t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}\sqrt{{(1)}^{2}+{(2t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}\sqrt{1+4{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 6
?

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=cos⁡(5t),y=6sin⁡(t) from t=0 to t=π2 (shown above)?

a
∫0π/225sin⁡(5t)+36cos⁡(6t)dt
b
∫0π/225sin⁡(t)+36cos2⁡(t)dt
c
∫0π/210sin2⁡(5t)+12cos2⁡(t)dt
d
∫0π/225sin2⁡(5t)+36cos2⁡(t)dt
e
2∫0π/25sin2⁡(5t)+6cos2⁡(t)dt
Submit

decision.explanation: The derivatives are x′=−5sin(5t) and y′=6cos(t). Thus the arc-length integrand √((x′)²+(y′)²) is √(25sin²(5t)+36cos²(t)). Integrating from 0 to π/2 gives option d.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14039829/assets/8868658c9bc7195f435a0109fce26b8a4fa39324c0a9a39e3fb644c5f02cdc9b.png)

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t),\,y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)$
from $t=0$ to $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ (shown above)?
after.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t))=-5\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))=6\operatorname{cos}⁡(t).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{(-5\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t))^{2}+(6\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{25{sin}^{2}⁡(5t)+36{cos}^{2}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6
?

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=cos⁡(5t),y=6sin⁡(t) from t=0 to t=π2 (shown above)?

a
∫0π/225sin⁡(5t)+36cos⁡(6t)dt
b
∫0π/225sin⁡(t)+36cos2⁡(t)dt
c
∫0π/210sin2⁡(5t)+12cos2⁡(t)dt
d
∫0π/225sin2⁡(5t)+36cos2⁡(t)dt
e
2∫0π/25sin2⁡(5t)+6cos2⁡(t)dt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To compute the arc length L of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

Computing the derivatives of x and y, we have

dxdt=ddt(cos⁡(5t))=−5sin⁡(5t) and dydt=ddt(6sin⁡(t))=6cos⁡(t).

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=∫0π/2(−5sin⁡(5t))2+(6cos⁡(t))2dt=∫0π/225sin2⁡(5t)+36cos2⁡(t)dt.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms option d: x′=−5sin(5t) and y′=6cos(t), so the speed is √(25sin²(5t)+36cos²(t)). Integrate this from 0 to π/2.

content.knowledge_point: Finding an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Parametric Curve Containing Special Functions
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14039829/assets/8868658c9bc7195f435a0109fce26b8a4fa39324c0a9a39e3fb644c5f02cdc9b.png)

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t),\,y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)$
from $t=0$ to $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ (shown above)?
content.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t))=-5\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))=6\operatorname{cos}⁡(t).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{(-5\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t))^{2}+(6\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{25{sin}^{2}⁡(5t)+36{cos}^{2}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 7
?

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=sin⁡(2t),y=sin⁡(3t) from t=π4 to t=π2 ?

a
∫π/4π/24cos2⁡(2t)+9cos2⁡(3t)dt
b
∫π/4π/22cos2⁡(2t)+3cos2⁡(3t)dt
c
∫π/4π/216cos2⁡(2t)+9cos2⁡(3t)dt
d
∫π/4π/22cos2⁡(2t)+9cos2⁡(3t)dt
e
∫π/4π/24cos2⁡(2t)+3cos2⁡(3t)dt
Submit

decision.explanation: By the chain rule, x′=2cos(2t) and y′=3cos(3t). The arc length integrates √((x′)²+(y′)²)=√(4cos²(2t)+9cos²(3t)) from π/4 to π/2, giving option a.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem:
Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$
from $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ to $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ ?
after.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))^{2}+(3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t))^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{4{cos}^{2}⁡(2t)+9{cos}^{2}⁡(3t)}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

after.html:
Question 7
?

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=sin⁡(2t),y=sin⁡(3t) from t=π4 to t=π2 ?

a
∫π/4π/24cos2⁡(2t)+9cos2⁡(3t)dt
b
∫π/4π/22cos2⁡(2t)+3cos2⁡(3t)dt
c
∫π/4π/216cos2⁡(2t)+9cos2⁡(3t)dt
d
∫π/4π/22cos2⁡(2t)+9cos2⁡(3t)dt
e
∫π/4π/24cos2⁡(2t)+3cos2⁡(3t)dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the arc length L of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

Computing the derivatives of x and y, we have

dxdt=ddt(sin⁡(2t))=2cos⁡(2t) and dydt=ddt(sin⁡(3t))=3cos⁡(3t).

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=∫π/4π/2(2cos⁡(2t))2+(3cos⁡(3t))2dt=∫π/4π/24cos2⁡(2t)+9cos2⁡(3t)dt.

content.knowledge_point: Finding an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Parametric Curve Containing Special Functions
content.problem:
Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$
from $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ to $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ ?
content.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))^{2}+(3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t))^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{4{cos}^{2}⁡(2t)+9{cos}^{2}⁡(3t)}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 8
?

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=2sin⁡(3t)−1,y=2cos⁡(2t)+2 from t=0 to t=π2 ?

a
2∫0π/29cos2⁡(3t)+4sin2⁡(2t)dt
b
2∫0π/26cos2⁡(3t)−2sin2⁡(2t)dt
c
4∫0π/2cos2⁡(3t)+sin2⁡(2t)dt
d
∫0π/29cos2⁡(3t)−4sin2⁡(2t)dt
e
2∫0π/26cos2⁡(3t)+2sin2⁡(2t)dt
Submit

decision.explanation: The derivatives are x′=6cos(3t) and y′=−4sin(2t). Thus the speed is √(36cos²(3t)+16sin²(2t))=2√(9cos²(3t)+4sin²(2t)). Integrating from 0 to π/2 gives option a.

after.name: Question 8
after.problem:
Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-1,\,y=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+2$
from $t=0$ to $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ ?
after.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-1) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\cdot 3 \\  & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+2) \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot 2 \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{(6\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t))^{2}+(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{36{cos}^{2}⁡(3t)+16{sin}^{2}⁡(2t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{9{cos}^{2}⁡(3t)+4{sin}^{2}⁡(2t)}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=2sin⁡(3t)−1,y=2cos⁡(2t)+2 from t=0 to t=π2 ?

a
2∫0π/29cos2⁡(3t)+4sin2⁡(2t)dt
b
2∫0π/26cos2⁡(3t)−2sin2⁡(2t)dt
c
4∫0π/2cos2⁡(3t)+sin2⁡(2t)dt
d
∫0π/29cos2⁡(3t)−4sin2⁡(2t)dt
e
2∫0π/26cos2⁡(3t)+2sin2⁡(2t)dt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To compute the arc length L of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

Computing the derivatives of x and y, we have

dxdt=ddt(2sin⁡(3t)−1)=2cos⁡(3t)⋅3=6cos⁡(3t) and dydt=ddt(2cos⁡(2t)+2)=−2sin⁡(2t)⋅2=−4sin⁡(2t).

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=∫0π/2(6cos⁡(3t))2+(−4sin⁡(2t))2dt=∫0π/236cos2⁡(3t)+16sin2⁡(2t)dt=2∫0π/29cos2⁡(3t)+4sin2⁡(2t)dt.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option a. Differentiating gives x′=6cos(3t) and y′=−4sin(2t), so the speed is √(36cos²(3t)+16sin²(2t))=2√(9cos²(3t)+4sin²(2t)). Integrate from 0 to π/2.

content.knowledge_point: Finding an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Parametric Curve Containing Special Functions
content.problem:
Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-1,\,y=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+2$
from $t=0$ to $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ ?
content.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-1) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\cdot 3 \\  & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+2) \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot 2 \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$

history.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-1) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\cdot 3 \\  & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+2) \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot 2 \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{(6\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t))^{2}+(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{36{cos}^{2}⁡(3t)+16{sin}^{2}⁡(2t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{9{cos}^{2}⁡(3t)+4{sin}^{2}⁡(2t)}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Differentiating gives x′=eᵗ and y′=eᵗ(sin(t)+cos(t)). The speed is eᵗ√(1+(sin(t)+cos(t))²)=eᵗ√(2+sin(2t)), since sin²(t)+cos²(t)=1. Integrating from −3 to 1 gives option a.

after.name: Question 9
after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14039829/assets/80577a585741748702b61596db84983592ecbc6c01fca78af033bf82dbe62ad2.png)

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x={e}^{t},\,y={e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t$
from $t=-3$ to $t=1$ (shown above)?
after.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})={e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)={e}^{t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{1}\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+{e}^{2t}{(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{1}{e}^{t}\sqrt{1+{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{1}{e}^{t}\sqrt{2+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=et,y=etsin⁡t from t=−3 to t=1 (shown above)?

a
∫−31et2+sin⁡(2t)dt
b
∫−31e2t1+cos⁡(2t)dt
c
∫−31et2+cos⁡(2t)dt
d
∫−31et1+sin⁡(2t)dt
e
∫−31e2t1+sin⁡(2t)dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the arc length L of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

Computing the derivatives of x and y, we have

dxdt=ddt(et)=et and dydt=ddt(etsin⁡t)=et(sin⁡t+cos⁡t).

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=∫−31e2t+e2t(sin⁡t+cos⁡t)2dt=∫−31et1+sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t+2sin⁡tcos⁡tdt=∫−31et2+sin⁡(2t)dt.

\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})={e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)={e}^{t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{1}\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+{e}^{2t}{(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{1}{e}^{t}\sqrt{1+{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{1}{e}^{t}\sqrt{2+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 10
?

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=sin⁡(t)−cos⁡(t),y=t−sin⁡(t) from t=0 to t=π4 ?

a
∫0π/41+sin⁡(2t)+2cos⁡(t)+cos2⁡(t)dt
b
∫0π/41+sin⁡(2t)+cos2⁡(t)dt
c
∫0π/42+sin⁡(2t)+cos⁡(t)−cos2⁡(t)dt
d
∫0π/42+sin⁡(2t)−2cos⁡(t)+cos2⁡(t)dt
e
∫0π/41+sin⁡(2t)−2cos⁡(t)dt
Submit

decision.explanation: The derivatives are x′=cos(t)+sin(t) and y′=1−cos(t). Their squared sum is 2+sin(2t)−2cos(t)+cos²(t), so the arc-length integral from 0 to π/4 matches option d.

after.name: Question 10
after.problem:
Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t),\,y=t-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)$
from $t=0$ to $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ ?
after.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))=\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{(\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))^{2}+(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡(t)+{sin}^{2}⁡(t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+1+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+1+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{2+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

after.html:
Question 10
?

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=sin⁡(t)−cos⁡(t),y=t−sin⁡(t) from t=0 to t=π4 ?

a
∫0π/41+sin⁡(2t)+2cos⁡(t)+cos2⁡(t)dt
b
∫0π/41+sin⁡(2t)+cos2⁡(t)dt
c
∫0π/42+sin⁡(2t)+cos⁡(t)−cos2⁡(t)dt
d
∫0π/42+sin⁡(2t)−2cos⁡(t)+cos2⁡(t)dt
e
∫0π/41+sin⁡(2t)−2cos⁡(t)dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the arc length L of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

Computing the derivatives of x and y, we have

dxdt=ddt(sin⁡(t)−cos⁡(t))=cos⁡(t)+sin⁡(t) and dydt=ddt(t−sin⁡(t))=1−cos⁡(t).

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=∫0π/4(cos⁡(t)+sin⁡(t))2+(1−cos⁡(t))2dt=∫0π/4cos2⁡(t)+sin2⁡(t)+2cos⁡(t)sin⁡(t)+1+cos2⁡(t)−2cos⁡(t)dt=∫0π/41+sin⁡(2t)+1+cos2⁡(t)−2cos⁡(t)dt=∫0π/42+sin⁡(2t)−2cos⁡(t)+cos2⁡(t)dt.

content.knowledge_point: Finding an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Parametric Curve Containing Special Functions
content.problem:
Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t),\,y=t-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)$
from $t=0$ to $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ ?
content.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))=\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{(\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))^{2}+(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡(t)+{sin}^{2}⁡(t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+1+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+1+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{2+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem:
Find the arc length of the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=2{cos}^{3}⁡t,\,y=2{sin}^{3}⁡t,\,t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].
$$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{cos}^{3}⁡t)=-6{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{sin}^{3}⁡t)=6{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length and get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{(-6{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(6{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{36{cos}^{4}⁡t{sin}^{2}⁡t+36{sin}^{4}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{36{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t){|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}(-1-1) \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the arc length L of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

Computing the derivatives of x and y, we have

dxdt=ddt(2cos3⁡t)=−6cos2⁡tsin⁡t and dydt=ddt(2sin3⁡t)=6sin2⁡tcos⁡t.

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length and get

after.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$

$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t-(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =t\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t-(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\  & =-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length and get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{(t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{t}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡t+{t}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{t}^{2}({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }t\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}\,{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{2}-0 \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the arc length of the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,t\in [0,\pi ].

after.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length and get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))}^{2}+{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡t-8\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+4{sin}^{2}⁡(2t)+4{cos}^{2}⁡t-8\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+4{cos}^{2}⁡(2t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{4+4-8(\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{8-8\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{8-8\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

According to the double-angle formula for cosine, $\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )=1-2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .$ Substituting $\theta =\frac{t}{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{t}{2}) & =1-2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2}) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t & =1-2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2}) \\ 1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t & =2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2}) \\ 8-8\operatorname{cos}⁡t & =16{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{8-8\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{t}{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & =-8{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{t}{2})|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =-8(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =-8(0-1) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}

EXPLANATION

To compute the arc length L of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

Computing the derivatives of x and y, we have

dxdt=ddt(2cos⁡t−cos⁡(2t))=−2sin⁡t+2sin⁡(2t) and dydt=ddt(2sin⁡t−sin⁡(2t))=2cos⁡t−2cos⁡(2t).

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length and get

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=∫0π(−2sin⁡t+2sin⁡(2t))2+(2cos⁡t−2cos⁡(2t))2dt=∫0π4sin2⁡t−8sin⁡tsin⁡(2t)+4sin2⁡(2t)+4cos2⁡t−8cos⁡tcos⁡(2t)+4cos2⁡(2t)dt=∫0π4+4−8(cos⁡tcos⁡(2t)+sin⁡tsin⁡(2t))dt=∫0π8−8cos⁡(2t−t)dt=∫0π8−8cos⁡tdt.

According to the double-angle formula for cosine, cos⁡(2θ)=1−2sin2⁡θ. Substituting θ=t2, we obtain

cos⁡(2⋅t2)=1−2sin2⁡(t2)cos⁡t=1−2sin2⁡(t2)1−cos⁡t=2sin2⁡(t2)8−8cos⁡t=16sin2⁡(t2)

Therefore,

∫0π8−8cos⁡tdt=∫0π16sin2⁡(t2)dt=4∫0πsin⁡(t2)dt=−8cos⁡(t2)|0π=−8(cos⁡(π2)−cos⁡0)=−8(0−1)=8.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14039829/assets/8288453c2625dac592a51054df332abf8ee49dbf8cbcabaf327c3ffe63b55f71.png)

Find the arc length of the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,t\in [0,\pi ].
$$
content.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length and get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))}^{2}+{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡t-8\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+4{sin}^{2}⁡(2t)+4{cos}^{2}⁡t-8\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+4{cos}^{2}⁡(2t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{4+4-8(\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{8-8\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{8-8\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

According to the double-angle formula for cosine, $\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )=1-2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .$ Substituting $\theta =\frac{t}{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{t}{2}) & =1-2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2}) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t & =1-2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2}) \\ 1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t & =2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2}) \\ 8-8\operatorname{cos}⁡t & =16{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{8-8\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{t}{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & =-8{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{t}{2})|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =-8(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =-8(0-1) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)) \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t),\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length and get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))}^{2}+{(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t))}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t-18\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+9{sin}^{2}⁡(3t)+9{cos}^{2}⁡t-18\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+9{cos}^{2}⁡(3t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{9+9-18(\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{18-18\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t-t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{18-18\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

According to the double-angle formula for cosine, $\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)=1-2{sin}^{2}⁡t.$ Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & =1-2{sin}^{2}⁡(t) \\ 1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & =2{sin}^{2}⁡(t) \\ 18-18\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & =36{sin}^{2}⁡(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{18-18\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{36{sin}^{2}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{\pi }|\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)|\,\text{d}t \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-6\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\,{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =-6(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =-6(-1-1) \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the arc length L of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

Computing the derivatives of x and y, we have dxdt=ddt(3cos⁡t−cos⁡(3t))=−3sin⁡t+3sin⁡(3t), and dydt=ddt(3sin⁡t−sin⁡(3t))=3cos⁡t−3cos⁡(3t).

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length and get L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=∫0π(−3sin⁡t+3sin⁡(3t))2+(3cos⁡t−3cos⁡(3t))2dt=∫0π9sin2⁡t−18sin⁡tsin⁡(3t)+9sin2⁡(3t)+9cos2⁡t−18cos⁡tcos⁡(3t)+9cos2⁡(3t)dt=∫0π9+9−18(cos⁡tcos⁡(3t)+sin⁡tsin⁡(3t))dt=∫0π18−18cos⁡(3t−t)dt=∫0π18−18cos⁡(2t)dt.

According to the double-angle formula for cosine, cos⁡(2t)=1−2sin2⁡t. Therefore, we obtain cos⁡(2t)=1−2sin2⁡(t)1−cos⁡(2t)=2sin2⁡(t)18−18cos⁡(2t)=36sin2⁡(t)

Therefore,

∫0π18−18cos⁡(2t)dt=∫0π36sin2⁡(t)dt=6∫0π|sin⁡(t)|dt=6∫0πsin⁡(t)dt=−6cos⁡(t)|0π=−6(cos⁡(π)−cos⁡0)=−6(−1−1)=12.
